blocks.text: J. Jeiteles shows in a longer essay in Kerem Chemed vol. 3, p. 98 ff., that the Talmudic שור הבר denotes neither the aurochs nor the buffalo, but either the humped ox (zebu) or the Tibetan buffalo. This view, however, suffers as much from contradictions as from false presuppositions. The aurochs is said to be domesticated, whereas Jeiteles himself reports from Funke that this animal is wild and untameable. Funke's claim, which Jeiteles accepts, that our domestic ox descends from the aurochs is incorrect, for the aurochs has 14 pairs of ribs, while the tame ox has only 13 pairs; the former is therefore by no means the ancestral race of the latter (cf. also Voigt l. c. 1, p. 423). — The presupposition that an animal does not confuse its instinct is false, since it is known that some species, e.g. the cat (perhaps also the horse, see Voigt ibid. p. 437), revert to the feral state although born in the tame state, which happens through a change of habitat. — After these refuted premises and claims, the reader of that essay will have to reject the view put forward there that שור הבר does not denote the aurochs.
מריא is said to be transposed from ראים (Jeiteles: Kerem Chemed vol. 3, p. 115).

Jonathan translates עגלה משולשת (Gen. 15, 9) by: עגלא ברת תלת שנין; whereas in Num. 19, 2 he renders the animal already in its second year by: תורתא, i.e., פרה. See on this my contribution in the L. Bl. d. Orients 1849, no. 24.

Joseph Karo, on Tur Eben ha-Eser §. 156, cites from the responsa of the Taschbaz several points which, while contradicting the statements of the Talmud, are different nowadays; thus cows and she-asses now bear young at two years and not, as the Talmud has it, only at three years. — The following words there are interesting: אעפ"י שאמרו יולדת לט' יולדת לשלמים כבר חמהו על זה רבים שהחוש מכויב זה והתו' כתבו שעתה נשתנו העניגים כמו שאמרו פ"ג דבכורות פרה וחמורה אינן יולדות אלא לג' שנים ועתה יולדות לב' שנים וכן תמצא בהרבה דברים.

The ancient manner of threshing is also described as follows. In the middle of the field a post was driven into the ground and a long pole was fastened to it in such a way that it could move freely around the post. Several cows were harnessed to this and first driven around in a circle on the spot until the ground was trodden firm. After the threshing floor had then been cleaned, the sheaves, which had previously been untied, were laid upon it and the animals were made to tread them out.
Cf. §. 81. It is expressly remarked that eating young poultry and milk produces a white and delicate complexion (Ketuboth 59b).

Swindlers knew how to give livestock intended for sale an artificial, apparent fatness for a short time; they watered the livestock with bran water (מי סובין), which made it bloated, so that its hair appeared, as with fat livestock, not lying flat but rather standing up. Other swindlers produced this standing of the hair by currying; both are of course forbidden (B. mez. 60b).

However, גמלא פרסאה might perhaps nevertheless be understood as the two-humped camel (Bactrian camel). Aristotle (Thierg. 2, 2, 5) calls the one-humped camel the Arabian camel, the two-humped the Bactrian camel, as does Pliny (h. n. 8, 18, 26); Bactria, as is well known, fell to the Persian empire, and so the Bactrian camel may be identical with גמלא פרסא.
In the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesachim 31a) it says: the male horse, both the castrated and the uncastrated, stands still when it wants to urinate (עומד ומשתין).

This Talmudic statement is properly understood only through the following quotation from the work מחזיק ברכה, which my brother Abr. Lewysohn communicates in his work מקורי מנהגים p. 69; it reads: שמעתי מה"ח מערי מערב הפנימי, שהיה זמן רב בדרך ודקדק כמה וכמה פעמים בשינה הסוס, והיה מונה נ"ט נשמי והסוס מתעורר, ועוד נ"ט נשמי והסוס מתעורר, ונ"ט נשמי דהסוס היו יותר מחצי שעה; accordingly the 59 or 60 breaths of the horse last over half an hour, and one breath of the horse as long as 59 breaths of a human.
עיר corresponds to the Greek Ὀρεύς [Oreus] and אתון to the Latin Asina.

Rashi (Rosch ha-Schana 3a) translates סיח by: עייר בן סום „foal of a horse“; more correctly Maimuni on the Mishnah (Sabbat 18, 2) by: עייר בן אתונות „foal of an ass“, likewise Bartenoro (B. batra 5, 3) and Heller (B. mez. 5, 4). — In B. batra 78b סיח is explained by מהלך אחר סיחה, i.e., as Samuel b. Meier adds, the young ass goes at the call of the driver, the old ass needs the whip.

On the other hand, in the Jozar for Sabbat-Sachor s.v. זכור the tribe of the Amalekite mountain people is designated with the words: איש אשר יושב נגב בלי עול כערוד „the dweller of the south, unsubjugated like the Arod“. Here there is probably an allusion to Rosch ha-Schana 3a, where the Canaanite is called ערוד במדבר; the latter expression is equivalent to חמור הבר „wild ass“.
